before.reason: The definition is for scalars and finite matrices with n>=1; it has no empty-domain instance.

after.evidence: Definition: For n=0, I_0 is the unique empty matrix; every power and partial sum is that matrix, and phi_k(0_0x0)=I_0/k!=0_0x0 including k=0.

changes.before: Definition: setting z=0 or X=0 leaves only the j=0 series term; lem-phi-series-converges-absolutely supplies the proved values.
changes.after: Definition: scalar zero gives 1/k!; positive-size zero matrices have only the j=0 term possibly nonzero, and at size0 every term is the empty matrix, yielding I_n/k! in every size.

changes.before: Definition: k=0 and every integer k>=0 are included; the matrix domain states n>=1.
changes.after: Definition: k=0 and every integer k>=0 are included; the matrix domain states n>=0, with I_0 the unique empty matrix.

changes.before: Put $R:=\|X\|_2$. The operator norm is defined by [F1]. Repeated submultiplicativity in [F2] gives $\|X^j\|_2\le R^j$, so $\|X^j/(j+k)!\|_2\le R^j/j!$ for every $j$. The norms therefore have a finite sum by [F4].
changes.after: If $n=0$, the series definition gives $X^j=I_0=0_{0\times0}$ for every $j\ge0$. Every term has norm $0$ by [F1], so the matrix series is absolutely convergent and every partial sum equals the unique empty matrix. For $n\ge1$, put $R:=\|X\|_2$. The operator norm is defined by [F1]. Repeated submultiplicativity in [F2] gives $\|X^j\|_2\le R^j$, so $\|X^j/(j+k)!\|_2\le R^j/j!$ for every $j$. The norms therefore have a finite sum by [F4].

changes.before: Let $S_N$ be the partial sums of the matrix series. For $N>M$, the triangle inequality bounds $\|S_N-S_M\|_2$ by the tail of the convergent scalar majorant in step 1.2, so $(S_N)$ is Cauchy. The matrix space is finite-dimensional and complete by [F3], hence $(S_N)$ converges in operator norm.
changes.after: For $n\ge1$, let $S_N$ be the partial sums of the matrix series. For $N>M$, the triangle inequality bounds $\|S_N-S_M\|_2$ by the tail of the convergent scalar majorant in step 1.2, so $(S_N)$ is Cauchy. The matrix space is finite-dimensional and complete by [F3], hence $(S_N)$ converges in operator norm. For $n=0$, convergence was established directly in step 1.2.

changes.before: At $z=0$ only the $j=0$ term of the scalar series is nonzero, and at $X=0$ only the $j=0$ matrix term is nonzero; these terms are respectively $1/k!$ and $I_n/k!$. Hence both stated zero values follow.
changes.after: At $z=0$ only the $j=0$ term of the scalar series is nonzero, and at $X=0$ with $n\ge1$ only the $j=0$ matrix term is nonzero; these terms are respectively $1/k!$ and $I_n/k!$. When $n=0$, every matrix term and $I_0/k!$ is the unique empty matrix by step 1.2. Hence both stated zero values follow for every allowed size.

before.reason: Statement assumes a finite matrix of dimension n>=1; there is no empty matrix-space case.

after.evidence: step 1.2: for n=0 every term has norm0, the series is absolutely convergent, and every partial sum is the unique empty matrix; step 2.1 retains this direct convergence case.

changes.before: Step 2.1 evaluates both scalar and matrix zero inputs directly.
changes.after: step 3.1 evaluates scalar zero, positive-size zero matrices and the empty matrix directly, using step 1.2 for the empty case.

changes.before: Step 1.2 applies to n=1 and the statement includes every finite n>=1.
changes.after: step 1.2 retains the positive-size norm majorant, including n=1; the Statement now includes every finite n>=0.

changes.before: The same index shift is valid in operator norm by [F2]; left multiplication by $X$ sends the $(j+k+1)!$ denominator term to $X^{j+1}/(j+k+1)!$. Thus $X\varphi_{k+1}(X)=\varphi_k(X)-I_n/k!$, proving the matrix recurrence.
changes.after: For $n=0$, every matrix term is the unique empty matrix by [F1], so the matrix recurrence is the equality of that matrix with itself. For $n\ge1$, the same index shift is valid in operator norm by [F2]; left multiplication by $X$ sends the $(j+k+1)!$ denominator term to $X^{j+1}/(j+k+1)!$. Thus $X\varphi_{k+1}(X)=\varphi_k(X)-I_n/k!$, proving the matrix recurrence.

changes.before: In $B_k(X,w)$, a block-product path from the first block row to the last column of the last block must move through the $w e_1^*$ block and then through all $k-1$ superdiagonal entries of $J_k$. It uses exactly $k$ block transitions; any remaining factors can only be copies of $X$ before that first transition. Hence the last column of the top-right block of $B_k^r$ is zero for $r<k$, and is $X^{r-k}w$ for $r\ge k$.
changes.after: For $n\ge1$, in $B_k(X,w)$, a block-product path from the first block row to the last column of the last block must move through the $w e_1^*$ block and then through all $k-1$ superdiagonal entries of $J_k$. It uses exactly $k$ block transitions; any remaining factors can only be copies of $X$ before that first transition. Hence the last column of the top-right block of $B_k^r$ is zero for $r<k$, and is $X^{r-k}w$ for $r\ge k$.

changes.before: By [F2] with $k=0$, $e^{B_k}=\varphi_0(B_k)=\sum_{r\ge0}B_k^r/r!$. By step 1.3, the last column of its top-right block is $\sum_{r\ge k}X^{r-k}w/r!=\sum_{j\ge0}X^jw/(j+k)!=\varphi_k(X)w$. This is exactly the first $n$ entries obtained by applying $e^{B_k}$ to the last coordinate vector.
changes.after: For $n\ge1$, by [F2] with $k=0$, $e^{B_k}=\varphi_0(B_k)=\sum_{r\ge0}B_k^r/r!$. By step 1.3, the last column of its top-right block is $\sum_{r\ge k}X^{r-k}w/r!=\sum_{j\ge0}X^jw/(j+k)!=\varphi_k(X)w$. This is exactly the first $n$ entries obtained by applying $e^{B_k}$ to the last coordinate vector. When $n=0$, $w$ is the unique vector in $\mathbb C^0$ and $B_k(X,w)=J_k$; the first zero entries of $e^{J_k}e_k$ and $\varphi_k(X)w$ are both the empty vector. Thus the augmented identity also holds in that case.

before.reason: Statement uses finite matrices with n>=1 and k>=0; there is no empty matrix domain.

after.evidence: step 1.2: at n=0 the recurrence is equality of the unique empty matrix with itself. step 2.1: B_k=J_k and the extracted first zero entries and phi_k(X)w are both the empty vector.

changes.before:
Use the first-variable-linear standard inner product on $\mathbb C^n$ and its norm $\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\sum_{i<n}|x_i|^2}$ from [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]] and [[def-inner-product-norm]]. The matrix norm $\|X\|_2$ is the operator norm of the linear map $x\mapsto Xx$ in [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].

For each integer $k\ge0$, define the scalar phi function and its finite-matrix action by

$$\varphi_k(z):=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^j}{(j+k)!},\qquad \varphi_k(X):=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{X^j}{(j+k)!}.$$

Here $z\in\mathbb C$, $X\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $n\ge1$, $X^0=I_n$, and factorials are the usual positive integer factorials. [[lem-phi-series-converges-absolutely]] establishes that both series converge absolutely for every such input, so these expressions define values on their full stated domains. By the published power-series definition [[def-complex-exponential]], $\varphi_0(z)=\exp z$; for matrices, $\varphi_0(X)$ is the bounded-operator exponential series of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]].

At zero, only the $j=0$ term remains, so $\varphi_k(0)=1/k!$ and $\varphi_k(0_{n\times n})=I_n/k!$.

The recurrence is always interpreted as a series identity, including at zero; division by $z$ is not part of this definition.

For every integer $k\ge0$, scalar $z\in\mathbb C$, and square matrix $X\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, the series-defined functions of [[def-phi-functions-by-everywhere-convergent-series]] satisfy
